###### Abstract

Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have led to
promising progress in web agents. However, existing web agents often
rely on handcrafted execution pipelines or expensive expert
trajectories, limiting their adaptability to complex, dynamic
environments. To address these challenges, we propose SCALE
(Self-Cognitive-Aware Learning and Exploration), which leverages three
adversarial roles—Selector, Predictor, and Judger to autonomously
discover the agent’s limitations and expand its cognitive boundaries
through environmental exploration. Moreover, we propose SCALE-Hop, a
graph exploration strategy that facilitates global planning and helps
agents avoid local exploration traps. To further support learning, we
construct SCALE-20k, a large-scale dataset collected from 19 real-world
websites, containing diverse task types and structured demonstrations
generated from SCALE’s exploration traces. Experimental results show
that our approach significantly improves the performance and
generalization of multiple MLLMs in various web environments. Our
framework offers a scalable and generalizable solution for building
truly autonomous and adaptive web agents.

## 1 Introduction

Recently, with the development of Multimodal Large Language Models
(MLLMs), MLLM-based web agents  \[[14](#bib.bib2), [34](#bib.bib6),
[33](#bib.bib10), [27](#bib.bib15)\] have demonstrated promising
performance in web automation tasks, like product
searching \[[11](#bib.bib5)\], shopping \[[35](#bib.bib4)\], and
navigation \[[15](#bib.bib3)\]. However, most existing web agents
heavily rely on the pre-trained capabilities of MLLMs, which are
difficult to cover large-scale and diverse web task
data \[[23](#bib.bib7), [2](#bib.bib35)\]. There remains a significant
gap between their prior knowledge and the highly varied and dynamic
real-world web pages. To address this gap, prior works usually depend on
the design of manually crafted execution pipelines \[[32](#bib.bib11),
[12](#bib.bib12), [7](#bib.bib13)\] or on the use of human-annotated
expert trajectories \[[30](#bib.bib1), [10](#bib.bib9), [29](#bib.bib8),
[3](#bib.bib18)\] for fine-tuning web agents.

![Refer to caption](2605.31365v1/figure_1.png)

Figure 1: A comparison between prior methods and our SCALE framework.
SCALE enables autonomous exploration with diverse and scalable task
generation, overcoming the limitation in previous approaches.

However, these two types of paradigms mentioned above still have notable
limitations: 1) Reliance on crafted execution pipelines or expert
trajectories. These methods either rely on crafted execution pipelines
for task execution or depend on costly expert trajectories to fine-tune
MLLMs \[[22](#bib.bib14), [27](#bib.bib15), [16](#bib.bib34)\]. Although
these pipelines and trajectories are often tailored for specific
scenarios, they still struggle to cope with the unpredictability and
diversity of real-world web environments \[[23](#bib.bib7),
[8](#bib.bib16), [26](#bib.bib19)\]. Agents in these paradigms tend to
act passively and develop dependencies on specific task flows, limiting
their ability to explore unfamiliar environments and adapt to dynamic
real-world websites. 2) Challenges in evaluating and expanding cognitive
boundaries. Cognitive boundaries are the limitations of an agent’s
abilities, referring to items and operations that the agent struggles to
understand or decide on based on prior knowledge \[[25](#bib.bib21)\].
It is significant for agents to improve their abilities. However,
existing methods have neglected the exploration of their own cognitive
boundaries. Therefore, how to evaluate and expand agent capabilities in
a personalized and dynamic manner remains a critical challenge. In
summary, developing general web agents requires enabling agents to
proactively adapt to novel environments and continuously expanding their
own cognitive boundaries, instead of relying on specific systems or
predefined trajectories.

To address these challenges, we propose SCALE (Self-Cognitive-Aware
Learning and Exploration), a general framework that removes reliance on
expert trajectories and handcrafted pipelines. SCALE enables agents to
autonomously discover and expand their cognitive boundaries through
self-driven interaction in web environments. Since it operates
independently of any specific model architecture, it offers broad
generalizability across different models. As shown in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning to Adapt: Self-Improving Web Agent via Cognitive-Aware Exploration"),
the agent proactively explores without external supervision by
identifying its own limitations, triggering exploratory actions in
uncertain areas, and adapting based on feedback. To evaluate and refine
its understanding, SCALE assigns three roles to the same MLLM: Selector,
Predictor, and Judger. The Selector proposes challenging actions, the
Predictor anticipates their outcomes, and the Judger verifies prediction
accuracy after execution. For example, the Selector may choose to click
a logo, believing the model is unsure about its effect. The Predictor
then estimates the outcome based on its current knowledge, expecting
nothing to happen. However, once executed, the Judger observes a jump to
the homepage, revealing a gap in the model’s understanding. This forms a
closed-loop process in which the Selector and Predictor engage in an
adversarial interaction, with one aiming to challenge the model and the
other aiming to predict correctly, while the Judger provides feedback to
improve both. The iterative process allows the agent to gradually adapt
to complex web environments.

Furthermore, we aim to enhance SCALE by extending its exploration
capability from local interactions to global reasoning and coordination.
We propose the SCALE-Hop strategy to complement it with global planning
and control. SCALE-Hop constructs a graph representation of the agent’s
interaction history, where each node represents a specific web state.
This graph allows the agent to monitor its exploration coverage and make
decisions at a higher level. When exploration becomes difficult or
complete at a given node, SCALE-Hop evaluates the model’s performance
and determines whether to exit and transition to another node that has
not been fully explored. This mechanism helps the agent efficiently
avoid local traps and supports a more comprehensive understanding of the
environment.

Based on the raw exploration traces from the SCALE process in 19
real-world websites, we construct SCALE-20k, a large-scale web task
dataset. Compared to existing datasets \[[22](#bib.bib14),
[29](#bib.bib8), [30](#bib.bib1)\], SCALE-20k offers not only execution
trajectories but also diverse task types, including multi-step tasks,
single-step decisions, and page comprehension QA, supporting more
comprehensive understanding and reasoning over web content.

Through comprehensive experimentation, our SCALE framework reveals that
MLLMs can proactively discover unknown aspects of the environment
through self-adversarial processes and achieve self-improvement by
continuously discovering and exploring these unknown aspects. Compared
to strategies that rely on random exploration or follow task
instructions rigidly, SCALE encourages the model to collect and update
data specifically in regions it does not yet understand. This leads to
more informative and error-revealing data, which better supports the
model’s improvement. Combined with the global route planning of
SCALE-Hop, it enables agents to move beyond shallow, localized behaviors
and form a more structured and comprehensive view of complex web
environments. Experimentally, SCALE achieves 231.8% improvement for
InternVL2.5-8B \[[4](#bib.bib31)\] and 176.3% improvement for
Qwen2.5-VL-7B \[[1](#bib.bib30)\] on average task success rate.
Furthermore, the SCALE-20k dataset achieves high scores in task
diversity, reasoning quality, and answer quality. Even when applied
directly to other MLLMs, SCALE-20k improves their agent capabilities.
These results further demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of
the SCALE framework.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

- •
  We propose SCALE, a self-driven learning and exploration framework
  that enables web agents to autonomously discover and expand their
  cognitive boundaries without relying on inference systems or expert
  trajectories.
- •
  We introduce SCALE-Hop, a dynamically adjusted exploration strategy
  according to the evaluation of cognitive boundaries, which facilitates
  broader content discovery and promotes the collection of more diverse
  and robust exploration.
- •
  We further provide SCALE-20k, a large-scale dataset derived from the
  SCALE exploration process, offering diverse task types, high-quality
  reasoning processes and answers to support future research on web
  agent understanding and reasoning.

![Refer to caption](2605.31365v1/figure_2.png)

Figure 2: The overview of SCALE and SCALE-Hop. SCALE consists of Input
Encoding, Self-Check, and Iterative Update. It enables agents to
identify unfamiliar actions, verify predictions, and iteratively improve

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Crafted Supervision for Web Agents

Early advances in MLLM-based web agents heavily rely on two forms of
external supervision: crafted execution pipelines and curated expert
trajectories. Crafted pipelines—such as
Tree-of-Thought \[[12](#bib.bib12)\], ReAct \[[32](#bib.bib11)\], and
world-model-based planning \[[7](#bib.bib13)\]—structure agent reasoning
through explicit modules (e.g., search or simulation) to guide actions.
While these enhance decision making, they require extensive manual
design and lack flexibility beyond pre-defined scenarios.

Meanwhile, approaches using expert trajectories depend on large
human-annotated datasets for real-world tasks. Data-centric works like
Mind2Web \[[6](#bib.bib22)\], Rico \[[5](#bib.bib23)\],
OSWorld \[[29](#bib.bib8)\], and AGUVIS \[[30](#bib.bib1)\] advance the
field, but face challenges in cost, diversity, and adaptability,
resulting in passive agents rigid to new settings. In contrast, our work
dispenses with handcrafted modules or costly labels, enabling agents to
self-assess and extend their abilities via autonomous exploration.

### 2.2 Adaptive Strategy for Web Agents

To address the rigidity of manual supervision, recent methods pursue
autonomous adaptation and self-improvement. Frameworks like
OpenWebVoyager \[[9](#bib.bib24)\] and AgentGym \[[28](#bib.bib25)\] use
iterative exploration and policy updates \[[17](#bib.bib20),
[18](#bib.bib26)\], yet usually require pre-defined task templates,
limiting adaptation.

Going further, exploration-based strategies such as
OS-Genesis \[[22](#bib.bib14)\] and
Learn-by-Interact \[[21](#bib.bib17)\] generate trajectories directly
through unsupervised interactions, retroactively creating tasks and
filtering via reward models. While this reduces task dependence, most
methods overlook systematically probing or expanding agent cognitive
boundaries. In contrast, our approach focuses on self-cognitive-aware
exploration, where agents autonomously identify, diagnose, and broaden
their own boundaries for robust environment adaptation.

## 3 Method

In this section, we first introduce the components and process of the
SCALE framework, and then further introduce SCALE-Hop’s graph
representation and verification-guided backtracking mechanism. Finally,
we introduce the construction method and analysis of the SCALE-20k
dataset.

### 3.1 SCALE

To move beyond handcrafted pipelines and expert trajectories, and to
enable agents to proactively identify and expand their own cognitive
boundaries in dynamic web environments, we propose a novel framework,
SCALE, that enables agents to proactively explore and adapt to web
environments without external supervision. In this part, we first
introduce its three key components: the Selector, Predictor, and Judger,
then describe the three core stages that facilitate cognitive boundary
assessment, followed by the formalized execution process of the
framework.

Selector, Predictor and Judger. The SCALE framework consists of three
essential components: Selector, Predictor, and Judger. These roles work
together to form a self-confrontation and self-verification mechanism,
enabling the agent to continuously identify and focus on actions that
are the most challenging to interpret within the current environment.
Importantly, all three roles are assumed and executed by the agent
itself, forming a fully self-contained reasoning and evaluation loop.

The Selector is responsible for identifying elements in the environment
that are likely confusing or rarely encountered by the agent, and
generating corresponding exploratory actions. For example, in a shopping
page, clicking a product is common and easy to understand. In contrast,
clicking the site logo is rare and less familiar. The Selector prefers
the latter to challenge the agent. Then, the Predictor is responsible
for analyzing the action and anticipating its expected outcome along
with an explanation. This enables the system to assess whether the agent
knows about the consequences of its decisions before execution. After
the action is executed, the Judger is responsible for comparing the
predicted outcomes to the actual results to determine whether the agent
truly understands the selected actions. These three roles interact in a
closed-loop that forms the foundation of the SCALE.

The process of SCALE. As illustrated in
Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning to Adapt: Self-Improving Web Agent via Cognitive-Aware Exploration"),
the operation of SCALE consists of three main stages: Input Encoding,
Self-Check, and Iterative Update. These stages work together to support
autonomous exploration, cognitive boundary assessment, and continual
adaptation.

Stage 1: Input Encoding In this stage, we adopt the commonly used
Set-of-Mark (SOM) technique \[[31](#bib.bib27)\] to process Graphical
User Interface (GUI) images. Unlike text-based methods that rely on
accessibility trees or HTML structures, our design processes purely
visual information. This choice is motivated by the fact that many
real-world websites restrict access to DOM or structural metadata,
whereas GUI images are always accessible. This design not only improves
the generalization ability of SCALE but also aligns more closely with
the way humans perceive and interact with the web through vision.

Stage 2: Self-Check In this stage, the Selector, Predictor, and Judger
collaborate to probe the agent’s current understanding of the
environment and actively search for its cognitive limits. The Selector
deliberately proposes challenging actions, targeting uncertain or
unfamiliar elements, whose outcomes the agent is least confident about.
While the Predictor attempts to anticipate the consequence of each
proposed action and explain why that outcome should occur based on its
existing knowledge. This creates an internal adversarial dynamic: the
Selector tries to expose behaviors the agent cannot yet understand,
while the Predictor strives to refute it by accurately forecasting the
true outcome. After the action is executed, the Judger compares the
predicted and observed results to decide whether the agent truly
understands the action’s effect. This self-supervised feedback loop
reveals where the agent’s understanding breaks down and localizes the
cognitive boundaries.

Stage 3: Iterative Update In this stage, the agent refines its reasoning
through iterative self-confrontation. Based on the judgments from the
Judger, actions with mismatched predictions are identified as failure
cases, which reveal aspects of the environment that the agent does not
understand. We focus on these failure cases rather than successful ones
because they expose the agent’s current cognitive limitations and
provide the greatest learning signal. These cases are then used to
update the Predictor, allowing it to learn the actual consequences of
previously misunderstood actions and acquire new knowledge about the
environment. Meanwhile, these cases also update the Selector, guiding it
toward actions that remain challenging. Through this mutually
reinforcing cycle, the Selector and Predictor co-evolve in a
self-improving manner, continually discovering new cognitive boundaries
and expanding the agent’s overall reasoning capability.

Formalized Execution Process. We denote the environment at step $`i`$ as
$`S_{i}`$, the observation as $`O_{i}`$, and the action as $`a_{i}`$,
where $`i\in[1,K]`$, and $`K`$ is the number of interaction steps in a
single self-update iteration. After $`K`$ steps, the agent undergoes one
round of self-update. Let $`j\in[1,N]`$ denote the number of self-update
rounds, with $`N`$ as the maximum number of updates allowed. For each
inner-loop iteration, the Selector first receives the current
observation $`O_{i}`$ and generates an action $`a_{i}`$:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       a_{i},r_{sel_{i}}=\pi_{sel_{j}}(O_{i})
       ```                                     |     |

where $`r_{sel_{i}}`$ is the reason for selecting $`a_{i}`$. This action
is then passed to the Predictor, which predicts its outcome:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       p_{i},r_{pre_{i}}=\pi_{pre_{j}}(O_{i},a_{i},r_{sel_{i}})
       ```                                                       |     |

where $`p_{i}`$ is the prediction of $`a_{i}`$, $`r_{pre_{i}}`$is the
reason for this prediction.

The action $`a_{i}`$ is then executed in the real environment
$`S_{i+1}=T(S_{i},a_{i})`$ and the agent receives the new observation
$`O_{i+1}=\Omega(S_{i+1}).`$ Next, $`O_{i}`$, $`O_{i+1}`$, and the
predicted outcome $`p_{i}`$ with explanation $`r_{pre_{i}}`$ are passed
to the Judger to determine whether the prediction was correct:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       j_{i}=\text{Judger}(O_{i},O_{i+1},a_{i},p_{i},r_{pre_{i}})
       ```                                                         |     |

where $`j_{i}\in\{0,1\}`$. If $`j_{i}=0`$, indicating that the
prediction was incorrect, the action is considered unfamiliar to the
agent and likely lies beyond its current knowledge boundary. In this
case, we use the Judger to generate the true outcome and explanation:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       t_{i},r_{t_{i}}=\text{Judger}(O_{i},O_{i+1},a_{i},r_{sel_{i}})
       ```                                                             |     |

where $`t_{i}`$ is the true description of the result of $`a_{i}`$,
$`r_{t_{i}}`$is the true reason for this description. Then we store this
exploratory data as
$`\text{ExploreData}_{j}^{i}=\langle O_{i},a_{i},r_{sel_{i}},t_{i},r_{t_{i}}\rangle`$.

If $`j_{i}=1`$, the action is deemed understood and provides no
cognitive improvement. The environment is then reset to $`S_{i}`$, and
the Selector generates a new action $`a_{i}^{\prime}`$:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
a_{i}^{\prime},r_{sel_{i}}^{\prime}=\pi_{sel_{j}}(O_{i},a_{i},r_{sel_{i}})
``` |  |

and the above process is repeated until an unfamiliar action
($`j_{i}=0`$) is generated.

After $`K`$ steps, all collected data
$`\text{ExploreData}_{j}=\{\text{ExploreData}_{j}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{K}`$ is
used to fine-tune the Selector and Predictor:

|     |                                                                  |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \pi_{sel_{j+1}}=\text{SFT}(\pi_{sel_{j}},\text{ExploreData}_{j})
       ```                                                               |     |

|     |                                                                   |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \pi_{pre_{j+1}}=\text{SFT}(\pi_{pre_{j}},\text{ExploreData}_{j}).
       ```                                                                |     |

Since the ability of judging is not trained during this process, the
Judger can be considered fixed during the iterative updates. The updated
policies $`\pi_{sel_{j+1}}`$ and $`\pi_{pre_{j+1}}`$ are then used for
the next round of exploration, enabling an iterative self-improvement
loop.

Through this process, the agent learns from unfamiliar knowledge and
expands its cognitive boundaries. Unlike task-driven methods such as
ReAct or tree search, SCALE performs self-driven exploration to
proactively adapt to new environments and discover boundary cases,
enabling higher-quality learning without extra inference-time
operations. The full iterative process algorithm and more details can be
found in Appendix A.

![Refer to caption](2605.31365v1/figure_3.png)

Figure 3: Overview of the SCALE-20k construction pipeline and
composition. The dataset is constructed in three stages: 1) Single-step
tasks are reverse-generated from valid exploration steps; 2) Multi-step
tasks are synthesized from coherent trajectories extracted via SCALE-Hop
graphs; 3) Page QA pairs are created to test content comprehension. The
dataset includes 19 real-world websites and supports three task types,
providing rich and diverse supervision for training web agents.

### 3.2 SCALE-Hop

Exploration in web environments involves not only exploring individual
pages and actions but also perceiving and navigating the environment as
a whole. However, relying solely on SCALE makes it difficult to obtain a
global perspective for exploration and correction. Accordingly, we
further propose SCALE-Hop, a global exploration strategy with high-level
planning and dynamic control. This section introduces its Graph
Representation and Verification-Guided Backtracking mechanism.

Graph Representation. As shown in
Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning to Adapt: Self-Improving Web Agent via Cognitive-Aware Exploration"),
SCALE-Hop models the agent’s exploration as a directed graph
$`\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{E})`$, where each node
$`n_{i}=(O_{i},u_{i})`$ represents a unique observation $`O_{i}`$ and
its URL $`u_{i}`$, and each edge $`e=(n_{i},a,n_{j})`$ denotes a
transition from $`n_{i}`$ to $`n_{j}`$ triggered by an action $`a`$,
where $`i,j\in[0,K]`$, and $`K`$ is the total number of nodes. To
distinguish different nodes, both the URL and the observation content
are considered. For a candidate environment, we first check whether its
URL has appeared before. If the URL is new, we directly create a new
node $`n_{\text{new}}=(O_{\text{new}},u_{\text{new}})`$ and add it to
the graph. If the URL already exists, we compare $`O_{\text{new}}`$ with
all observations of nodes sharing the same URL using the Structural
Similarity Index (SSIM), only when all SSIM scores are below a
predefined threshold $`\delta`$ do we treat it as a new environment and
insert a new node into the graph. During exploration, the graph is
dynamically constructed and refined. It provides a compact and
expressive way to record the agent’s exploration history, enabling
efficient tracking of visited regions, recognition of novel states, and
subsequent global planning over the environment.

Verification-Guided Backtracking. To further enhance the agent’s global
exploration capability, we propose the Verification-Guided Backtracking
mechanism as a core component of SCALE-Hop. Each node in the exploration
graph is dynamically assigned one of three states: Unexplored, Partially
Explored, or Fully Explored, reflecting the agent’s current
understanding of that local environment. The transition between these
states is driven by continuous verification of prediction accuracy and
exploration coverage.

When local exploration stalls or appears complete, a verification phase
is triggered. The agent samples $`N`$ random actions from the current
node and uses the Predictor to predict their outcomes. If all
predictions match the actual results, the node is marked as Fully
Explored, otherwise, it remains Partially Explored for further
investigation. Once the verification is passed, the agent then
backtracks to the nearest node that is still Unexplored or Partially
Explored. This mechanism balances broad exploration with strategic
focus, helping the agent make steady and meaningful progress across
diverse web environments.

Through the combination of Graph Representation and Verification-Guided
Backtracking, SCALE-Hop performs logically consistent and globally aware
exploration, avoiding getting trapped in local regions and missing
globally valuable areas. This design enables the SCALE framework to
maintain comprehensive and balanced coverage across the entire web
environment.

### 3.3 SCALE-20k

Since high-quality web task data are both scarce and expensive to
obtain, based on the exploration conducted by SCALE across 19 real-world
websites, we construct the SCALE-20k dataset. We first introduce three
stages for constructing the dataset, and then analyze its composition
and statistics.

Dataset Construction Pipeline. As shown in
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 SCALE ‣ 3 Method ‣ Learning to Adapt: Self-Improving Web Agent via Cognitive-Aware Exploration"),
based on the exploration data obtained from SCALE, we leverage GPT-4o to
assist in task construction and validation, and construct the dataset
through the following three stages.

Stage 1: Single-Step Task Generation From the SCALE exploration process,
we collect numerous valid exploration actions. Then we reverse-construct
a corresponding single-step task and reasoning processes based on this
action.

Stage 2: Multi-Step Task Generation To reflect the complexity of
real-world tasks, we extract coherent multi-step trajectories from the
SCALE-Hop graph. The logically validated trajectory is then used to
reverse-construct the corresponding task and reasoning process.

Stage 3: Page Comprehension QA Pair Generation To enhance the agent’s
understanding of web environments, we generate question-answer pairs for
each node in the SCALE-Hop graph, providing rich page-level supervision
that strengthens the agent’s comprehension and reasoning ability.

Dataset Composition and Statistics. As shown in
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 SCALE ‣ 3 Method ‣ Learning to Adapt: Self-Improving Web Agent via Cognitive-Aware Exploration"),
SCALE-20k comprises exploration data collected by Qwen2.5-VL-7B and
InternVL2.5-8B across 19 real-world websites. It includes 15042
single-step tasks, 3780 multi-step tasks, and 6886 page comprehension QA
tasks.

## 4 Experiments

In this section, we first describe the experimental setup, then present
the main results, followed by an in-depth analysis of the experiments.

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

Baselines. We select Qwen2.5-VL-7B \[[1](#bib.bib30)\] and
InternVL2.5-8B \[[4](#bib.bib31)\] as backbone models to evaluate our
method. We used GPT-4o as a representative closed-source baseline. We
also compare against strong open-source agents, including Augvis, a
vision-only GUI agent \[[30](#bib.bib1)\], and ViGoRL, a vision-based
reinforcement learning agent \[[20](#bib.bib28)\]. Beyond zero-shot
settings, we consider three enhanced strategies: 1) Imitation learning
on GPT-4o successful trajectories, 2) OS-Genesis exploration
method \[[22](#bib.bib14)\], which constructs tasks from randomly
explored trajectories, and 3) Tree Search strategy that explores
multiple reasoning paths during inference time via a tree structured
search. To further validate the effectiveness of our proposed SCALE-20k
dataset, we additionally include a model that is entirely unrelated to
our exploration model, LLaVA‑NeXT‑8B \[[13](#bib.bib33)\], and fine-tune
it directly on SCALE-20k.

Evaluation Benchmarks. We conduct evaluations on two widely-used web
agent benchmarks: VisualWebArena and WebVoyager. VisualWebArena covers
diverse domains such as shopping, classifieds, and forums, while
WebVoyager includes real-world websites with complex layouts and
dynamic, real-time content changes. For WebVoyager, we test on the first
11 tasks of each website to ensure consistency. To enable a fair
comparison across all methods, we unify the input format by using only
webpage screenshots with visual markup as the observation. All other
auxiliary information, such as accessibility trees and page
descriptions, is removed. Further experimental details are provided in
Appendix B.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|

### 4.2 Main Results

Through comprehensive experimentation, we validate the effectiveness and
generalization of our proposed method:

Effectiveness of SCALE. The SCALE framework is effective across MLLMs of
different scales. As shown in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Adapt: Self-Improving Web Agent via Cognitive-Aware Exploration"),
both InternVL2.5-8B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B demonstrate the ability to
autonomously explore web environments in SCALE. As a result, they
achieve average performance improvements of 231.8% and 176.3% over their
vanilla counterparts. In addition, SCALE significantly outperforms other
open-source vision-language agents such as Augvis, and ViGoRL across
most environments. This validates the effectiveness of SCALE in
enhancing the agent’s capabilities. Moreover, the consistent
improvements across different models suggest that our method is general
and can be applied to a wide range of MLLM backbones.

Beyond vanilla zero-shot baselines, SCALE outperforms two mainstream
improvement paradigms—expert-trajectory supervision and manually
engineered reasoning pipelines. Compared with models trained on GPT‑4o
trajectories or OS‑Genesis exploration data, SCALE achieves consistently
better or competitive performance, often reaching or surpassing
state-of-the-art results. Its advantage is particularly notable on
WebVoyager, where dynamic content and diverse page layouts make static
or manually curated trajectories insufficient, highlighting SCALE’s
stronger generalization and adaptability.

In terms of efficiency, we report the average number of steps (AS) taken
across all tasks, regardless of success. As shown in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Adapt: Self-Improving Web Agent via Cognitive-Aware Exploration"),
SCALE achieves the lowest or second-lowest AS in most domains,
indicating more concise and effective reasoning paths compared to
trajectory-based or tree-search baselines.

Moreover, as shown in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Adapt: Self-Improving Web Agent via Cognitive-Aware Exploration"),
increasing the number of SCALE iterations leads to consistent
performance gains, indicating that deeper exploration enables the agent
to discover more informative behaviors and improve task success rates.

### 4.3 In-Depth Analysis

In this section, we further analyze how SCALE enables deeper and broader
exploration.

Ablation Study: The Importance of Self-Adversarial Interaction in
Exploration. We observe that the self-adversarial mechanism in SCALE
plays a vital role in enhancing exploration behavior. As shown in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Adapt: Self-Improving Web Agent via Cognitive-Aware Exploration"),
our method significantly outperforms random walk in both task success
rate (SR) and exploration coverage. It consistently visits more unique
nodes with higher diversity in URL distribution and visual layout. Many
of these nodes lie in rarely accessed regions—such as footer menus,
hidden tabs, and domain edges—that are often overlooked by goal-driven
or randomly sampling agents. This demonstrates that self-adversarial
interaction is key to enabling not only deeper exploration, but also
continual self-driven improvement.

Ablation Study: Contribution of SCALE-Hop.
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Adapt: Self-Improving Web Agent via Cognitive-Aware Exploration")
further highlights the impact of SCALE-Hop within the framework. Its
integration yields the largest performance improvement across
environments, boosting both SR and the number of visited nodes. On
average, SCALE-Hop increases node coverage by 216% compared to the w/o
SCALE-Hop setting, enabling the agent to escape local patterns and
uncover a wider range of states. This confirms SCALE-Hop as a crucial
driver of long-horizon, diverse, efficient, and self-improving
exploration.

Diversity of the SCALE-20k. To evaluate dataset diversity, we compute
the average cosine distance between Sentence‑BERT \[[19](#bib.bib29)\]
embeddings of task descriptions. In addition, we assess dataset quality
using GPT‑4o along two complementary dimensions, reasoning quality and
answer quality, with evaluation prompts detailed in Appendix C. As shown
in
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Adapt: Self-Improving Web Agent via Cognitive-Aware Exploration"),
SCALE‑20k achieves strong performance across all three metrics,
exhibiting higher semantic diversity and better reasoning-action
correctness than other datasets. Moreover, as shown in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Adapt: Self-Improving Web Agent via Cognitive-Aware Exploration"),
even a model unrelated to our framework (LLaVA‑NeXT‑8B) gains clear
improvements when fine‑tuned solely on SCALE‑20k, further demonstrating
the effectiveness and generality of our dataset.

Case Study. As shown in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Adapt: Self-Improving Web Agent via Cognitive-Aware Exploration"),
this case demonstrates how SCALE’s components collaboratively identify
the agent’s cognitive boundary. On the left, although the selected
action (clicking the product) is valid, the Predictor already
understands its outcome well, suggesting this interaction is within the
agent’s current knowledge and offers limited exploratory value. On the
right, a new action (clicking “Advance Search”) is selected. The
Predictor’s expectation is invalidated by the Judger, signaling a gap in
understanding. This mismatch reveals a gap in understanding and drives
targeted exploration, showcasing SCALE’s ability to recognize and expand
cognitive boundaries.

Towards Lifelong Exploration via Self-Adaptation. As exploration
progresses, the agent gradually improves its ability to handle complex
interfaces without external supervision—each update relies solely on
internal judgment and feedback. As shown in
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Adapt: Self-Improving Web Agent via Cognitive-Aware Exploration"),
both task success rate and exploration diversity increase steadily. This
illustrates a promising direction toward lifelong exploration learning,
where agents continuously adapt to evolving web environments through
self-driven feedback loops.

## 5 Conclusion

In this work, we propose SCALE, a self-driven framework that enables web
agents to autonomously explore and expand their cognitive boundaries
without relying on handcrafted pipelines or expert demonstrations. It
uses the Selector, Predictor, and Judger to collaboratively form
internal feedback loops, enabling the agent to identify and overcome its
cognitive limitations. At the global level, we design the SCALE-Hop
strategy to guide broader and more strategic exploration across diverse
web environments. Additionally, we construct SCALE-20k, a large-scale
and diverse dataset, from SCALE trajectories. Experimental results
demonstrate the effectiveness and adaptability of our approach for
building general web agents.

## Appendix A Details of SCALE Framework and SCALE-20k Dataset

This section provides a comprehensive overview of the formal definition,
algorithm, and implementation details of the SCALE framework, as well as
the construction of the SCALE-20k dataset. It covers the POMDP
formulation, the iterative self-check algorithm, prompt designs for each
module, exploration-specific parameters, and representative dataset
examples to facilitate reproducibility.

### A.1 Formulation of the SCALE

We model the exploration process as a partially observable Markov
decision process (POMDP), defined as a tuple $`(S,A,O,T,R,\Omega)`$,
where $`S`$ denotes the set of environment states, $`A`$ is the action
space, including actions such as Click, Type, Hover and Scroll, and
$`O`$ represents the set of observations available to the agent.
$`T:S\times A\rightarrow S`$ is the state transition function that
models how the environment changes in response to an action, and $`R`$
is a binary function used to determine whether an exploration action is
worth performing in a given state. $`\Omega:S\rightarrow O`$ is the
observation function that maps the underlying state to the observable
interface. This formulation captures the uncertainty and partial
observability inherent in real-world web environments.

### A.2 Algorithm of the SCALE Framework

This is the specific algorithm of the SCALE method. We denote the
environment at step $`i`$ as $`S_{i}`$, the observation as $`O_{i}`$,
and the action as $`a_{i}`$, where $`i\in[1,K]`$, and $`K`$ is the
number of interaction steps in a single self-update iteration. After
$`K`$ steps, the agent undergoes one round of self-update. Let
$`j\in[1,N]`$ denote the number of self-update rounds, with $`N`$ as the
maximum number of updates allowed. The algorithm is shown in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ A.2 Algorithm of the SCALE Framework ‣ Appendix A Details of SCALE Framework and SCALE-20k Dataset ‣ Learning to Adapt: Self-Improving Web Agent via Cognitive-Aware Exploration").

0:  Initial policies $`\pi^{sel}_{1}`$, $`\pi^{pre}_{1}`$, fixed Judger,
max update rounds $`N`$, steps per round $`K`$, initial state $`S_{1}`$

1:  for $`j=1`$ to $`N`$ do

2:   Initialize buffer: $`\mathcal{D}_{j}\leftarrow\emptyset`$

3:   for $`i=1`$ to $`K`$ do

4:    $`O_{i}\leftarrow\Omega(S_{i})`$

5:    $`(a_{i},r^{sel}_{i})\leftarrow\pi^{sel}_{j}(O_{i})`$

6:    repeat $`\leftarrow`$ True

7:    while repeat do

8:
    $`(p_{i},r^{pre}_{i})\leftarrow\pi^{pre}_{j}(O_{i},a_{i},r^{sel}_{i})`$

9:     $`S_{i+1}\leftarrow T(S_{i},a_{i})`$

10:     $`O_{i+1}\leftarrow\Omega(S_{i+1})`$

11:
    $`j_{i}\leftarrow\text{Judger}(O_{i},O_{i+1},a_{i},p_{i},r^{pre}_{i})`$

12:     if $`j_{i}=0`$ then {Action not understood}

13:      repeat $`\leftarrow`$ False

14:     else {Action understood, try again}

15:      $`S_{i+1}`$ is reverted to $`S_{i}`$

16:
     $`(a_{i},r^{sel}_{i})\leftarrow\pi^{sel}_{j}(O_{i},a_{i},r^{sel}_{i})`$

17:     end if

18:    end while

19:
   $`(t_{i},r^{t}_{i})\leftarrow\text{Judger}(O_{i},O_{i+1},a_{i},r^{sel}_{i})`$

20:
   $`\mathcal{D}_{j}\leftarrow\mathcal{D}_{j}\cup\{(O_{i},a_{i},r^{sel}_{i},t_{i},r^{t}_{i})\}`$

21:   end for

22:
  $`\pi^{sel}_{j+1}\leftarrow\text{SFT}(\pi^{sel}_{j},\mathcal{D}_{j})`$

23:
  $`\pi^{pre}_{j+1}\leftarrow\text{SFT}(\pi^{pre}_{j},\mathcal{D}_{j})`$

24:   $`S_{1}\leftarrow S_{K}`$

25:  end for

Algorithm 1 Self-Check and Iterative Update Process

### A.3 Exploration Specific Parameters

We define several key parameters in the SCALE-Hop module to support
effective exploration and verification in web environments.

Node Differentiation. To determine whether two nodes represent different
web states, we jointly consider the URL and the visual similarity
between observations. Specifically, we compute the Structural Similarity
Index Measure (SSIM) between the two screenshots. A new node is created
only if the URL differs or the SSIM value is below a strict threshold of
0.99, ensuring that visually similar pages are not redundantly
revisited.

Verification-Guided Backtracking. To avoid infinite loops in local
exploration, we introduce a self-verification mechanism. If the agent
remains within the same node for more than 10 consecutive steps without
successful progression, it triggers Verification-Guided Backtracking.
During this process, the system generates 5 candidate verification
actions to determine whether the current state has been misunderstood or
overlooked due to subtle changes in the environment. When there is link
fluctuation or the exploration becomes stuck and difficult to continue,
the self-verification mechanism is proactively activated to trigger
verification-guided backtracking and switch to another node.

Think Process Prompt In task-oriented web environments, reasoning about
the next action based on the current observation is essential for agent
decision-making. We design think process prompts to help the model infer
the immediate intention behind the first action in a given task context.

While different types of tasks may involve different reasoning
strategies depending on task structure and action dependencies, we unify
the prompt format across examples with slight variations depending on
action ordering. Here, we present the think process prompt tailored for

## Appendix B Detailed Experimental Setup

In this section, we provide detailed descriptions of the experimental
settings to facilitate reproducibility. We first introduce the baselines
and benchmarks, then outline the evaluation protocol, and finally detail
the hardware and training settings for
Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct \[[1](#bib.bib30)\],
InternVL2.5-8B \[[4](#bib.bib31)\] and
LLaVA‑NeXT‑8B \[[13](#bib.bib33)\].

### B.1 Baselines and Evaluation Benchmarks

Baselines. To comprehensively evaluate the effectiveness of our method,
we compare against the following categories of baselines:

Closed-source Model. We include GPT-4o, a strong commercial
vision-language agent accessed via OpenAI’s official API. All GPT-4o
evaluations are conducted in a strict zero-shot setting, without
additional training or in-context demonstrations. This serves as an
upper bound reference.

Open-source Agent Model. We evaluate against two representative
open-source agents:

- •
  Augvis \[[30](#bib.bib1)\]: a unified vision-based GUI agent that
  operates directly on raw screen images and performs cross-platform
  tasks through standardized visual interactions. Augvis is trained on a
  large-scale multimodal dataset with GUI grounding and reasoning
  annotations. It achieves strong performance on both offline and
  real-world benchmarks without relying on closed-source models.
- •
  ViGoRL \[[20](#bib.bib28)\]: a vision-language agent trained via
  reinforcement learning to perform spatially grounded reasoning. It
  anchors each reasoning step to specific visual coordinates and
  dynamically adjusts visual attention through multi-turn RL. This
  design enables effective fine-grained exploration and visual
  decision-making across complex GUI environments.

Backbone Models. Our method is implemented on two strong open-source
multimodal foundation models: InternVL2.5-8B and Qwen2.5VL-7B-Instruct.

Enhanced Training or Inference Strategies. To further investigate the
web agent capabilities of the models, we apply three widely used
enhancement strategies on top of the above backbones:

- •
  GPT Trajectory Fine-tuning: We fine-tune the agent using successful
  trajectories obtained from GPT-4o on the evaluation tasks. These
  trajectories are collected by running GPT-4o in the test environments
  and extracting correct responses. As a result, this strategy
  introduces a powerful form of supervision, especially effective in
  improving performance on tasks the model has seen during fine-tuning.
- •
  OS-Genesis \[[22](#bib.bib14)\]: This setting uses the OS-Genesis-Web
  dataset, which is employed to fine-tune the model. The dataset is
  constructed by having an agent randomly explore synthetic websites and
  then automatically reverse-construct corresponding tasks and aligned
  trajectories. The dataset contains high-quality expert demonstrations
  across various domains (e.g. shopping, reddit and classifieds).
- •
  Tree Search Inference \[[12](#bib.bib12)\]: A manually crafted
  inference pipeline that enables language model agents to perform
  multi-step planning in interactive web environments. To ensure
  experimental efficiency, we adopt the following setup: the agent
  generates five candidate actions at each step and selects two valid
  ones for simulation. The resulting states are evaluated using the
  model itself as a value function, and only high-scoring paths are
  retained while low-value branches are pruned. The search is performed
  with a depth of three steps. This method supports strategic
  exploration and multi-step reasoning during inference without
  requiring any additional training.

SCALE. We leverage the SCALE framework to collect trajectory data
through autonomous interaction with corresponding web environments. It
enables agents to explore, assess, and adapt beyond their cognitive
boundaries in dynamic and unfamiliar web settings. Based on these, we
use another model to construct structured tasks (e.g., single-step,
multi-step, QA), which are then used to fine-tune the base model. This
enables the agent to improve through its own experience without relying
on human annotations.

SCALE-20k. To further evaluate the effectiveness of our collected
SCALE-20k dataset, we fine-tune another model,
LLaVA‑NeXT‑8B \[[13](#bib.bib33)\], which has a different architecture,
directly on the data collected by Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and
InternVL2.5-8B, and compare its performance with its own baseline.

Evaluation Benchmarks. We evaluate our method and baselines on two
established benchmarks: VisualWebArena \[[11](#bib.bib5)\] and
WebVoyager \[[8](#bib.bib16)\], which together cover both predefined and
real-world web environments.

- •
  VisualWebArena: VisualWebArena includes evaluation tasks from three
  representative websites, Shopping, Classifieds, and Reddit, along with
  a small number of cross-domain tasks. For each individual website, we
  exclusively train the agent on the data collected by SCALE within that
  website’s environment, ensuring that evaluation remains
  domain-specific. To account for varying website complexity, we set the
  maximum exploration depth to 60-25, where the agent runs up to 60
  self-update rounds with 25 interaction steps each. Since
  over-exploration may introduce noisy actions, we evaluate models
  trained with different exploration depths and report results from the
  depth with the highest validation success rate.
- •
  WebVoyager: WebVoyager is a large-scale benchmark designed for
  evaluating web agents in real-world websites. In our experiments, we
  evaluate on all 15 websites in WebVoyager, using the first 11 tasks
  from each site to construct a comprehensive evaluation suite. For data
  collection, SCALE is used to explore each site at depths 10-25, where
  the agent runs up to 10 self-update rounds with 25 interaction steps
  each. We then combine exploration data from all 15 websites to train a
  general-purpose agent for evaluation. Due to the lack of official
  GPT-4o trajectories and the limited generalizability of Tree
  Search-style methods to highly dynamic and diverse real-world
  websites, we exclude those two baselines from this benchmark.

Input Standardization: To ensure consistency across all methods and
backbones, we standardize the input format for all agents. Specifically,
we remove all auxiliary metadata (e.g., accessibility trees or HTML DOM
representations) provided by the original benchmarks and retain only the
visual screenshot and its corresponding set-of-mark
(SOM) \[[31](#bib.bib27), [24](#bib.bib32)\]. For different model
backbones, image resolution is automatically adjusted to meet the input
size constraints, ensuring stable inference across evaluation settings.

### B.2 Training Hardware and Hyperparameters

Hardware. During the exploration phase, we used a total of 8 GPUs for
SCALE deployment, model training, and updates. All training and
evaluation experiments are conducted on NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs. We utilize
2 or 4 GPUs for model fine-tuning and inference.

Training Hyperparameters. We fine-tune three different vision-language
models in our experiments: Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, InternVL2.5-8B and
LLaVA‑NeXT‑8B.

Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct: We fine-tune the model using the LLaMA Factory
framework with LoRA-based supervised fine-tuning. The main
configurations are as follows:

- •
  LoRA: Applied to all modules with rank 8.
- •
  Input: Images resized to a maximum of 921,600 pixels; token cutoff
  length set to 4096.
- •
  Batching: 2 GPUs, with per-device batch size 1 and gradient
  accumulation of 8.
- •
  Optimization: Learning rate 1e-4, cosine decay, warmup ratio 3%, 15
  training epochs. Select approximately 1000 steps checkpoint for
  testing (the checkpoint that performed best during training).
- •
  Precision: bf16 and FlashAttention v2 enabled.

InternVL2.5-8B: We follow the official LoRA training pipeline with the
following key hyperparameters:

- •
  LoRA: Only LLM is fine-tuned with LoRA (rank 8); vision backbone, MLP,
  and LLM weights are frozen.
- •
  Input: Dynamic image resolution with thumbnails enabled; forced image
  size set to 448; max dynamic patch is set to 4.
- •
  Batching: 2 GPUs, with per-device batch size 1 and gradient
  accumulation of 8.
- •
  Optimization: Learning rate 1e-4, cosine schedule, weight decay 0.05,
  warmup ratio 3%, 10 training epochs.
- •
  Precision: bf16 training with gradient checkpointing enabled.

LLaVA‑NeXT‑8B: We fine-tune the model using the LLaMA Factory framework
with LoRA-based supervised fine-tuning. The main configurations are as
follows:

- •
  LoRA: Applied to all modules with rank 8.
- •
  Input: Images resized to a maximum of 921,600 pixels; token cutoff
  length set to 4096.
- •
  Batching: 4 GPUs, with per-device batch size 1 and gradient
  accumulation of 8.
- •
  Optimization: Learning rate 1e-4, cosine decay, warmup ratio 3%, 15
  training epochs. Select approximately 500 steps checkpoint for testing
  (the checkpoint that performed best during training).
- •
  Precision: bf16 and FlashAttention v2 enabled.

## Appendix C Quality Evaluation of SCALE-20k

In this section, we first introduce three metrics for evaluating dataset
quality and provide corresponding evaluation prompts.

### C.1 Evaluation Metrics

To evaluate the diversity and quality of the SCALE-20k dataset, we adopt
three complementary metrics:

Task Diversity. We follow the procedure described in the main paper and
embed each task description using Sentence-BERT \[[19](#bib.bib29)\]. We
then compute the average pairwise cosine distance between all task
embeddings. A larger average distance indicates greater semantic
variation across tasks, reflecting broader coverage of task types.

Reasoning Quality. To assess the quality of the agent’s reasoning, we
employ GPT-4o as an automatic evaluator. For each task instance, the
evaluator is given the task objective, the generated reasoning, the
proposed next action, and screenshots for context. GPT-4o scores the
reasoning on a 1-10 scale by examining whether it is accurate, concise
when appropriate, free of hallucinations, and tightly aligned with the
proposed action and task. A brief justification is produced together
with the numerical score. The final reasoning quality score is obtained
by averaging the GPT-4o scores across all instances and linearly mapping
the result to the 0-1 range.

Answer Quality. Similarly, to evaluate the correctness and
appropriateness of the agent’s proposed next action (or final answer),
we employ GPT-4o as an automatic evaluator. For each task instance, the
evaluator is given the task instruction, the assistant’s reasoning and
action, and screenshots. GPT-4o scores the answer on a 1-10 scale by
examining whether the action is valid for the current observation,
follows all agent side constraints (e.g., one action at a time,
whitelist-restricted action types, and required output format), and
constitutes the best or near-best step toward accomplishing the
objective. A brief justification is produced together with the numerical
score. The final answer quality score is obtained by averaging the
GPT-4o scores across all instances and linearly mapping the result to
the 0-1 range.

In summary, these three metrics jointly capture the semantic diversity
of tasks and the quality of reasoning and actions, providing a
comprehensive assessment of the SCALE-20k dataset.

quality are provided below.
